comparison: Perfect agreement on epistasis experiments (C3, C4, C43, C44). Both evaluations accept the genetic evidence showing LDLR and APOE dependence of the SEC24A cholesterol phenotype without challenge.
Complete agreement on tissue-specific deletion data (C34, C35, C36). Both accept that hepatic SEC24A loss is sufficient to reduce plasma cholesterol and acknowledge the liver-specific mechanism.

Strong agreement on viability and developmental data (C1, C23-C26). Both evaluations accept that SEC24A deficiency has no apparent effect on viability or development, describing it as a 'strikingly restricted phenotype.'
Complete agreement on hypocholesterolemia findings (C2, C30-C33). Both evaluations accept the reduced cholesterol measurements as convincing and reproducible across multiple experimental conditions.

Disagreement on therapeutic implications (C83, C85, C87). OpenEval considers claims speculative but reasonable pending human validation, while peer reviewers explicitly state therapeutic potential should be de-emphasized and is premature given other phenotypic effects.

Disagreement on COPII-dependent PCSK9 secretion (C6, C51-C54). OpenEval finds convergent evidence from multiple approaches sufficient, while peer reviewers require additional direct mechanistic experiments (SEC24A knockdown in budding assays, liver cytosol from knockout mice).

Disagreement on SEC24A-PCSK9 selectivity (C55-C59). OpenEval accepts co-IP, overexpression, and siRNA data as sufficient evidence, while peer reviewers require direct mechanistic link through knockdown experiments in the budding assay system.

Disagreement on PCSK9 retention mechanism (C46-C49). OpenEval finds the Endo H sensitivity and protein localization data coherent and sufficient, while peer reviewers express concerns about data quality (PCSK9 blot quality, cross-reactive bands) and request additional antibody validation.

Disagreement on LDLR mechanism (C5, C45). OpenEval accepts the increased hepatic LDLR data as part of coherent mechanism, while peer reviewers request ruling out other mechanisms affecting LDLR levels (specifically IDOL E3 ligase).

Agreement on broader COPII cargo selectivity implications (C8, C66, C73, C76). Both evaluations accept that findings demonstrate differential requirements for COPII subunits and describe the selectivity as remarkable and of general interest.

Agreement on SEC24A/B functional overlap (C7, C60, C61, C70) and partial agreement on genetic interactions. Both accept the genetic and biochemical evidence for partial redundancy between SEC24A and SEC24B paralogs.
Agreement on lack of SEC24A-SEC24D genetic interaction (C62-C65). Both evaluations accept the compound mutant data showing functional distinction between SEC24D and SEC24A/B subfamilies.

Disagreement on SREBP pathway effects (C37, C38). OpenEval accepts transcriptome and q-PCR data as ruling out general cholesterol biosynthesis disruption, while peer reviewers note other phenotypic effects (>50% SCD1 mRNA reduction) suggesting broader secretory impacts.

Agreement on RBC phenotype (C27). Both evaluations accept the mild increases in RBC MCV and MCHC as real phenotypic effects, though peer reviewers use this to support concerns about therapeutic implications.

OpenEval evaluated SEC24 paralog expression characterization (C39-C42) showing similar protein levels despite different transcript levels and lack of compensatory upregulation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.
OpenEval evaluated tolerance to combined SEC24A/B reduction (C86) showing viability of compound mutants. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim.
